## Seat lifecycle controls and metadata (2026-10-16)

Socket `pause` and `resume` remain rejected through `UNAVAILABLE`, including for the host. The existing host-side `RoomRuntime` pause APIs remain available without a public client caller. The server owns the supplied wall-clock deadlines and the one-second pause/frame cadence; the deterministic core receives no timer. Paused ingress ignores new orders while preserving the queue for resume. Operative and AI room admission remain closed on R1.

Every admitted seat receives the existing roster-ordered `online` and `ping` arrays, as in reference `e4e579a` (`server.js:504,774`, `server/room-tick.js:30`). AI seats project `true` and `-1`, and unknown human RTT stays null. The common frame sender applies these fields to scheduled, paused and catch-up delivery without changing recipient visibility or wire shape.

AI-19 evidence covers the existing detached core state: lazy spawn camera, private RNG, sampled opening delay and explicit resets through ordinary ticks and both recipient snapshots. It does not enable room AI or its takeover/departure callers. Only AI-19 and NET-66 are claimed. NET-79 is dropped because socket pause/resume ingress needs owner approval. NET-80 remains outside the proven set because live AI handover and loaded-save pause need separate activation and save work.

## Tutorial runtime over existing Match systems (2026-10-16)

The explicit `Match::new_tutorial` constructor adds the unattended Enemy seat and uses the existing `tutorial_steps` definitions. Tutorial shares the ordinary ground, routing, combat, objective and support systems. Its private step state owns only the current index, spawned IDs and pending dialogue. Lines leave through the core tick report from tick 40; no server or client transport is introduced. The runner advances at most one step per tick after capture and income, and finishes at the bridgehead through the common Match finish state.

Instant Tutorial recruitment reuses the existing admission, debit and unit-publication transaction, with a separate home-placement path because Tutorial has no production buildings. The public Conquest production component keeps its existing mode gate. Tutorial reinforcements use the player's spawn and exclude the unattended enemy. The prototype's 5 MP/s base income and lack of a defeat condition are preserved. Public server admission, agreed interfaces and parity statuses stay unchanged.

## Interface collection order and recipient queries (2026-10-16)

Field hospitals use insertion order plus keyed membership, matching the prototype's Map semantics. Replacing an owner preserves placement order; removing and rebuilding a hospital appends it. World transactions clone both parts, and recovery and logistics consume the ordered iterator. Existing fire, soak, contact, navigation and live ascending-unit traversal keep their native implementations, with focused consumer tests for each collection. The hospital test advances an ordinary one-VP match through victory and three subsequent ticks, capturing complete snapshots for every seat without a fault. The World training test exercises the existing live unit loop without changing World admission or claiming World snapshot delivery.

Availability and denial queries borrow only the reconstructed recipient ClientView. Map presentation helpers consume only the supplied received map; authoritative map validation still uses its stricter layer validation. The pure queries compare against pinned JavaScript fixtures, while collection tests assert the prototype's traversal intent. ABI exports and Unreal adoption remain separate. No header, wire, contract, privacy or public ingress change is included.

Concrete cells use the existing finished-building publisher so their unit, control, combat, firing, ability, recovery, production and terrain records share the normal Match owners. The paid job retains its bounded occupancy retry count. A separate step-back goal keeps a deferred crew escape valid when the deterministic path budget is exhausted. This preserves the intended four-metre escape on a later tick without changing wall cost, build time or retry limits.

Waiting Dig orders use the existing unit queue and ordinary paid Dig activation. The recipient adapter emits the existing engineering order kind for those waiting orders. Default/Conquest admission remains bounded; Classic and World field-work rooms stay guarded. No FFI, header, wire schema, contract or privacy policy changes.

## AI shopping construction inputs (2026-10-16)

Shopping receives the remaining budget and the reserves produced by the same detached planning pass. The observation no longer carries estimated build and fortification reserve amounts or a precomputed free-node count. Public resource positions, delivered depot memories and explicit owned-node indices provide the inputs. Node claims use only delivered depots and remembered enemy depots, at strictly less than eight metres. World engineer demand counts every unclaimed delivered node; its construction reserve considers only nodes on delivered owned ground.

Construction and fortification proposals use the existing canonical command path. Builders assigned earlier in the pass remain busy, so later movement cannot replace their new jobs. Fortification still computes its reserve after base construction or repair. Assigned workers stay excluded, and proposed building positions join the fortification site exclusions so two jobs cannot spend against overlapping footprints. A delivered own-worker wall-work fact distinguishes wall Dig from ordinary Dig when deciding whether another crew may fortify. Candidate and worker ties use stable node indices and unit IDs. Fortification progress belongs to the existing private per-seat policy state, outside Match and recipient snapshots. Wall fortification dispatch remains separate work. Gate Dig remains unsupported at command admission. The planner computes their reserve thresholds but emits neither command and charges neither cost.

The live observation producer remains limited to Default and Conquest. Classic and World shopping and reserve decisions can be exercised with detached inputs; this does not admit those modes or complete their construction and observation providers. Full construction, fortification and FireAt chores remain separate parity work. No FFI, C header, wire, contract or privacy change is included.

## Runtime engineering: native bridge identity (2026-10-16)

Paid bridges and Fill use the existing field-work jobs and canonical World mutations. Newly constructed bridge graphs use deterministic identities derived from the first cell and the append-only structure count. Repair reuses an existing bridge section identity, restores wood and 200 HP, and reconnects neighboring sections. These graph identities stay separate from the shared actor ID allocator, so construction does not advance actor IDs. Support, terrain invalidation and hull-width queries continue to use the canonical graph and physical terrain. This is an internal identity choice; no new wire or ABI shape is introduced.

# Three Crossroads Native: design decisions

## Private Horde director queue (2026-10-16)

The core seat dispatcher selects the human commander for ordinary seats and a
scripted director for the internal Horde seat. The director retains its latest
detached observation, uses Normal's 40-tick stagger and drains movement on every
delivered observation beat. Live wave state prevents an old observation from
dispatching after a break, wave replacement or match finish.

Pending Horde movements belong to the director, outside canonical unit order
queues. Each emitted movement is an ordinary single-unit command attempt for
the existing admission path. Typed owner intent, including native route identity,
replaces the prototype's JSON fingerprint. A same-cell Move or idle Stop changes
that identity and invalidates pending work. Replacing a queued unit preserves its
FIFO position; all callbacks for one observed tick share a four-order allowance.
This adds core components without admitting full Horde ticking, recipient
snapshots or hosting. Full-match lifecycle coverage uses an ordinary Conquest
match with a detached wave context and the existing recipient snapshots.

## Typed scenario conditions and core refunds (2026-10-16)

Scenario condition evaluation borrows typed authored state while reading current units, point owners and World region teams from Match. A caller supplies the context and shares an explicit work budget across evaluations. This keeps condition reads separate from scenario admission, trigger scheduling, actions and recipient projection. The evaluator follows the pinned condition semantics, including historical captures, pending arrivals, context fallback and short-circuit work charges. A 64-level guard protects callers that construct trees directly; validated authored trees remain below it.

Waiting-job refunds prepare small production and wallet drafts before publishing the negative MP-spent tally. Site cancellation uses the existing World transaction before the wallet, story and metadata cleanup commit. These core operations add no network admission. Full MODE-91 remains held beyond the selected refund and recovery checks. MODE-83 proves the condition component, not an admitted authored-scenario match.

## Editable map drafts and bounded save preparation (2026-10-16)

Map authoring uses an in-memory draft separate from `World` and `Match`. Selection moves retain the selected layer's material overrides and authored section identities, health and supports. Failed bounds or collision checks leave the draft unchanged. Removal and support pruning can leave an invalid draft, which must pass the ordinary map validator before saving. This keeps unsupported surviving sections visible as authoring errors instead of silently repairing their anchors.

The map loader now calls the scenario validator added in #298. A validated scenario can be edited and prepared for saving, but every startup profile rejects explicit authored scenarios before creating match state because their executor is absent. The previous fixture assertion that scenarios were unsupported by the loader now checks their retained definition. No command, event, flag or other live match state was added.

`map_save::prepare_map_save` applies the prototype's save-field projection and an 8 MiB limit to incoming bytes before parsing, including discarded properties. It prepares bytes in memory and validates the projected document again. HTTP editor authorization, persistence and server integration remain absent, so MAP-23 remains component-only. The existing 16 MiB authoritative-loader limit is unchanged. Generated World documents are outside the demonstrated save scope. MAP-57's rendered-ground sampler and MAP-90's station-yard construction integration remain unimplemented; World admission stays guarded. MAP-92 retains field-specific diagnostics and stronger bounded integer checks for region IDs and ordered bounds, reported as differs candidates rather than approved differences.

PR #214 at `ee7bdc3c899b912f229dade7e5d58855052d87b7` separates lint, tests and release into three jobs on each of Ubuntu 24.04, Windows 2025 and macOS 15, for nine jobs total. Nextest runs each test in its own process and schedules across binaries, whereas local `cargo test` shares process state within each consolidated integration binary. [Axel decision 085](https://github.com/axelmanosalvasmd/ww2-rts-native/issues/5#issuecomment-6178373888) explicitly accepts both changes, conditional on fresh exact-head hosted checks. Review 084's process-state request is addressed here: a static scan of the core/simtest test trees found no mutable globals or environment, working-directory or logger mutations matching the checked patterns. Each job restores a dependency cache using Swatinem/rust-cache 2.9.2 pinned at `6323deb102c322ba6fcbdcafc7e3dddab59af2b6`. Only trusted `main` runs save; PR runs restore without saving. Separate lint/test/release keys also include OS, architecture, toolchain/environment and dependency-lock hashes. This keeps simtest's Git-provenance build fresh. Cold-cache PR runs before a main save do not demonstrate a warm-cache gain.

## Consolidated integration test binaries (2026-10-14)

PR #213 builds the 40 `ww2-core` and 56 `ww2-simtest` integration test files as two binaries, one `tests/it/main.rs` per crate. Each existing file remains a module. Both manifests disable automatic test discovery and declare the `it` target explicitly. Simtest helpers shared by several files compile once under `tests/common`, accessed through `crate::shared::*`. Each crate's `every_test_file_is_compiled` guard compares the top-level test files with the actual path/module declarations and rejects an additional `tests/<dir>/main.rs` target. `ww2-ffi` retains its three test files and the approved header's `--test header` invocation.

The decision reduces separate compilation and linking while retaining the existing tests and assertions. Plain `cargo test` now runs a crate's former integration binaries in one process. Source inspection at `3b9b7d5d` found no mutable process-global test state or environment/current-directory mutations in the consolidated test files and helpers. ## World movement without a memory copy when movement reads none (2026-10-14, Vostro)

Each World ground move used to prepare a private copy of the team's remembered terrain before moving: it cloned `WorldMemory`, refreshed every visible cell and rebuilt route knowledge, then discarded the copy unless movement read terrain or asked for a route. For a team with no memory yet (the local defender on the first move of a tick) that is a full rebuild of all 91,700 cells of the `world_tick` map, about 70 ms. Counters over the first eight steps of `world_tick::original_world_steps_use_the_actual_runner_and_explicit_whole_admission` showed 1,720 such preparations, 211 of each step's 215 for team -1, and every one started from an empty memory.

`move_world_unit_without_memory` now runs the same movement step first on a copy of the unit, with physical traffic terrain whose every read marks a flag and a route callback that only records that it was called. If movement read no terrain and requested no route, its result cannot depend on remembered terrain, so it equals what the prepared path would produce; the trial is kept with the same grid update, reinsertion and cached-unit update the prepared path performs when it reads nothing. Otherwise the trial is dropped (Game and the grid are untouched until a trial is kept) and the unchanged prepared path runs. The context validation the prepared path performs first runs on both paths.

A temporary differential check ran the prepared path on a snapshot after every kept trial and required bit-identical `Moved`, units and grid, and that the prepared path committed no memory: 12,469 moves matched in `world_tick` and 248 in the rest of the workspace, with 1 fallback. Vostro, `ci-test`: that test took 972 s before the change, 51.7 s in the first focused run on pre-base-update head `e59059e60b8b9427b227aeb22d08a23e559f42c9`, and 53.9 s in the workspace run on acknowledged final head `624357c23c8f7183b0738014d60d23bd314270b0`.

## Recoverable changelog collection (2026-10-14)

The collector's initial Git deletion preflight cannot reserve the index.
A late index lock after changelog replacement left the fragments present,
and a retry copied their bullets again. Before replacement, the collector
now publishes a private per-worktree Git journal containing the complete
original and assembled changelog, NUL-separated fragment paths, exact
fragment contents and original NUL-separated Git index entries (blob, mode,
stage and path). Changelog replacement uses a temporary file on its own
filesystem. Each invocation requires exclusive access to the worktree,
fragment paths and its Git index. No new locking tool is required.

When validated, a retry accepts only the recorded original or assembled
changelog,
unchanged remaining fragments and their recorded index entries. From the
original state it replaces the changelog; from the assembled state it resumes only the owned fragment
removals. Already removed fragments are skipped. The journal survives
process interruption and Git deletion failure and is removed only after
all owned deletions finish. Unrelated changelog, fragment or index edits
present when checked refuse recovery until the recorded state is
restored. The collector never removes Git's index lock. Identity is the
fragment path and exact contents, not bullet text, so distinct fragments
with identical bullets both survive collection. New fragments wait for the
next invocation after recovery.

The first recovery candidate checked only worktree contents. A staged
replacement whose worktree file was subsequently removed could therefore
pass Git's deletion check and be lost. Recovery now verifies every remaining
index entry's exact blob, mode, stage and path before any fragment removal,
even when the worktree file is missing. A changed staged entry present when
validated refuses recovery, retaining the index, journal and assembled
changelog. A missing
worktree file with the original index entry may still recover normally.

A separate review showed that one collector alone does not reserve the
index: another Git writer can stage a replacement and remove its worktree
file after validation, and the collector's later deletion can remove that
replacement. The checks and actual git rm are separate operations, not one
atomic transaction. Each invocation therefore requires exclusive access to
the worktree, fragment paths and Git index, with all other Git and worktree
writers waiting until it exits. The guards check changes present at
validation, including changes made between retry invocations; concurrent
changes after those checks are unsupported.

Final order remains newest date on top, with same-date topic filenames in
descending order, retaining the existing insertion and spacing rules. This
clarifies Axel review 084 and owner decision 085. Their process-sharing note
is addressed by recommending local nextest after test-binary consolidation:
plain cargo test shares a process across formerly separate test files,
whereas nextest isolates each test. This collector follow-up changes no test
layout, Cargo profile, runtime, workflow or interface.

Collector validation passed 26 owned-scratch checks: 25 current-script
behavior checks and one reproduction of the earlier index-loss bug. The
current-script checks cover exact output against the original collector,
ordering, dirty-input refusal, post-replacement process kill, late index
lock, partial deletion, recovery
refusal after unrelated edits, repeated no-op, identical legitimate bullets,
new fragments arriving during recovery, unusual quoted paths and linked
worktree isolation. The added index checks retain changed blobs, modes and
conflict stages on refusal, then recover after the original index entry is
restored. These checks do not cover concurrent writers. This documentation
correction preserves all script commands and prior verification receipts,
with no Cargo or native runs.

This is a bounded quiet opening/holder, later research-attempt and Germany MG purchase checkpoint, not full strategic AI, completed research, construction, mass-project Cover or a complete match. The new human observation/state/planner work is not part of this published stack.

The earlier local acceptance remains exact compiled `e7f1b1f`: 25 affected debug tests, 227 locked workspace release tests, strict Clippy, formatting, release FFI and 50 independent copied-test executions. Those results do not establish the merged head. Fresh Linux, Windows and macOS checks on the published combined head are required before Root merges; Unreal acceptance and remaining privacy/product decisions stay separate.

## Why native (2026-10-11)

Measured in ww2-rts:

- **Server:** one battle's tick runs on one thread. A heavy Conquest battle (Six Fronts, six Massive AI, about 400 units) costs 16.3 ms mean and 34.0 ms p95 of the 50 ms tick in Node (`tools/bench.mjs`, ww2-rts#58). Bun is 1 to 14% faster. `WW2_SHARDS=N` (`server/shards.js`) spreads separate rooms over processes, but nothing splits one battle.
- **Client:** the browser's main thread draws, builds terrain and runs game logic. A three-human Huge World Conquest session fell to 0.7 FPS; after the ww2-rts#61 fixes it runs at about 30 FPS on an RTX 4060 with 12.6 ms of frame-loop JavaScript.
- **Crowds:** 2,160 soldiers near the camera run at about 35 FPS on Low and 21 to 23 on High in the ww2-rts#64 synthetic fixture; the GPU spends 22 to 41 ms a frame on that scene.

The goal is thousands of units per battle and a public release later. ww2-rts#64 concluded its own measurements don't justify a rewrite, so step 1 measures before anything is ported.

## Architecture (2026-10-11, pending step 1)

Paid construction uses `UnitControl.build_target` for the source's numeric site identity and `Unit.build` only as its synchronized activity projection. Sites reuse Game progress/health, World footprints/sections and ProductionState queues. Typed Build pays and stamps immediately even when queued, recording a singleton Assist with the snapped site center in the existing waiting queue. The path scheduler retains the source's live Build goal, including a present dead site until the actual worker turn clears it; exhausted retries drop only the site scalar and its projection. Accepted replacement and pre-drop retirement use the existing field owner cancellation with the paired construction cleanup. No paid site is refunded or deleted by replacing its workers.

One temporary ConstructionFrame captures site and worker membership at actual unit turns, preserving first-site and turn order. Its finish phase runs before the late captured unit list and does not reselect workers after movement or damage. Completion keeps the full crew/buildTime/tick expression even when progress clamps at one, so a site can need another repair turn before its workers clear their target. Finished repair uses the canonical section actuator and ordered provision debits. All touched logging layers, section reads, aggregate mutation/journal capacity and story charges validate before publication.

Accepted rare placement prepares a temporary physical World and maintained grid plus the recipient, Fog and path caches used by its crew. A private Arc shares the sole immutable InitialTerrain allocation; initial() stays unchanged. The checked cache fork rebinds recipient flags/heights and owned vehicle buffers while retaining graph versions, incremental history, serials and search scratch. The draft stamps levels and cells, creates the actual newborn and footprint graph, then routes crews in original order. Local routing acknowledges only draft pending records. The final physical guard binds dimensions, source allocation, revisions, ledger epoch/end and pending sets, then publishes into existing live terrain allocations. Wallet, story, ID and control writes follow all fallible preparation. Queued crews perform no route query and retain the original live routing caches. Immediate route publication clears only those crews' existing retry failure rows, as source findPath does; pending requests and failed/queued operations remain intact. Empty fires preserve the source's lazy Fog behavior; a same-key warm Fog stays warm with its original frame. There is no whole-Match or per-tick clone, new job authority, second queue, or RNG reset.

The unmodified source recorder covers 29 cases, 113 commands/scene actions, 1,919 full steps and 2,013 snapshots. Constructor seed pairing supplies the existing source draw from Match seed 701's Weather stream; runtime environment state advances naturally. A declared disabled-logistics reserve scene witnesses exact repair budgets, residual floats and the first-missing-reserve debit break. The native consumer is written against advance_tick, not copied phase logic, but requires the sole runner owner's construction wiring before proof. This checkpoint remains source-only until final source review and coherent native gates. The current caller admits only Default/Conquest with absent Game.mode and the eight static ground kinds. Depot nodes, coastal/cache providers, site cancellation/refund and Classic/World integration remain subsequent production work; no ABI, transport or player rule is changed.

Mass-project tick admission reads the existing canonical project and paid-work owners before the clock changes. Its temporary set verifies complete current actor membership without sorting the caller's turn sequence or keeping a captured actor store. Listed and archived active counters are checked under the exact source recount gate; stale queued Join numbers remain ordinary command denials. An unmodified full-step source recorder adds seven cases, 193 steps and 215 snapshots for actual payment, crew/sweep, death, completion and retry-drop timing. At `914efe7`, four debug admission guards, all 214 release workspace tests, strict Clippy, formatting and release FFI passed after both-profile package cleans. Independent copied debug and release binaries each passed the four guards. The source steps remain evidence for later sole-runner composition, with no native full-tick result or second tick implementation claimed.

Mass field projects use the single FieldWorksRuntime owner for unpaid ordered segments, unit membership and paid Dig records. Monotonic project IDs let BTreeMap retain source creation order; segment Vec order preserves middle-first allocation and strict first-distance ties within the next crew-sized window. A source-listed project can become archived while unit references still need its identity. Cancellation removes membership and paid work together without a refund, while cached active/crew counters keep the source recount timing. Typed Match admission and phase providers share the existing command queue and paid-cell executor. A failed Dig route drops only paid work; accepted replacement commands cancel membership too. The original recorder covers 216 plans, 40 prices and 25 traces (137 actions, 162 snapshots). Native comparison passes for 168 supported plans, 30 prices and 23 Match traces (131 actions); direct-helper and unsupported Wall cases stay explicit. Compiled `0f17e93` passed 13 focused debug checks, all 210 release workspace tests, strict Clippy, formatting and release FFI, with independent source and debug/release review. Full runner assembly, client previews and recipient works rows remain separate; engineering rows stay in progress.

Two programs talking over the network, as today. Only the rules core decides outcomes.

1. **Rules core (Rust, `rust/crates/core`).** Port of `shared/`. 20 ticks a second. The same seed gives the same match. Unit, weapon and map tables live in data files both sides read. No engine, networking or file-system code.
2. **Room host (`ww2-server`, Rust).** One thread per room; a battle's tick is split across cores and merged in a fixed order. AI planning and long path searches run on worker threads and apply at a fixed future tick, so the battle never waits and results stay deterministic. It runs standalone on Windows or Linux, or the game's Host button starts it as a separate program.
3. **Protocol.** Today's WebSocket protocol first, so the browser client works against the Rust server during the switch. Later:
   - your own units arrive as orders plus occasional corrections;
   - enemy units arrive as positions, only while seen;
   - binary and versioned;
   - UDP through relays for public release.
4. **Unreal 5.8 client.** Drawing, HUD, effects, sound and input only. It links the core through a C interface generated by cbindgen for the rules the browser client imports today: 56 names from `shared/sim.js` (55 still used) across 35 client files, 86 names from all of `shared/` across 40, such as `placementCheck`, `canBuild`, `priceOf`, `popCap`, `CELL`, `UNITS`, `CFG`. It also uses the core to move your own units between updates.

## Two repos (2026-10-11)

Axel chose a separate repo for the native rebuild. To keep the native game measured against the JavaScript game:

- ww2-rts stays the playable game, and gameplay changes keep landing there.
- `reference/ww2-rts` is a submodule pinned to a ww2-rts commit (`e4e579a` at creation). `PARITY.md` lists what that commit does and how the native game is measured against it.
- Moving the pin is its own commit, with the port of the changed rules and the affected `PARITY.md` rows updated.

## The JavaScript game is a prototype (2026-10-12)

Julio's direction: the JavaScript game was a prototype for trying the game's ideas out, and nothing in it is set in stone. The native game keeps every feature and its intent, and improves the architecture, engineering and rules wherever it can, instead of copying the JavaScript bit for bit.

- Inside the Rust core and server, improvements need only a record here. Changes players would notice also mark their `PARITY.md` row `differs` and need Axel's agreement, since issue #4 makes behavior differences a joint decision.
- Exact comparison with the JavaScript stays where it is cheap and finds port bugs: data tables, pure functions, single-component fixtures. Whole matches are compared by outcomes agreed before the run.
- Why: copying the prototype exactly would mean copying its accidents. At the pin, one unseeded random stream is shared by every room in a process, the AI's view of the battle refreshes on a beat set by measured server time, and some unit choices depend on the spatial grid's bucket order. None of these is a design choice, and each makes matches impossible to replay. `PARITY.md` lists the proposed replacements (decisions 1 to 8).

## Reference pin (2026-10-12)

`e4e579a` stays the working pin for step 1 (#2, #3) and for `PARITY.md`. Julio and Axel choose the porting pin together at the #1 decision (Julio's ack `julio-coordination-001` on #5). The only later ww2-rts commit on 2026-10-12, `d71532c` (#66), speeds up the browser client's drawing, adds an opt-in WebTransport motion lane and fixes save loading; its `shared/` edits give the same results by inspection.

## Thousands of units

A unit is a squad or a vehicle; an infantry squad draws 15 soldiers. Four pieces are needed, and a line-by-line port won't provide them:

1. **A tick that uses every core:** vision, movement, combat and snapshots split across cores, then merge in a fixed order.
2. **Group pathfinding:** a group heading to one place shares one flow field (a map of directions toward the goal), so cost follows destinations, not units.
3. **Orders instead of positions** for your own units, which keeps the host's upload small.
4. **Cheaper crowds:** animation baked into textures and less detail with distance. This needs measuring, because the ww2-rts#64 browser experiment that moved animation work to the GPU came out slower.

## Cheating

The server is the referee and each player receives only what their own units can see.

- **Blocked by design:**
  - map hacks: hidden units, terrain and enemy plans are never sent;
  - speed, teleport, resource and health edits: those values live only on the server;
  - illegal orders: refused whole;
  - reading enemy routes and targets: they go to their owner only.
- **Needs more:**
  - host cheating: host matches that matter on a dedicated or official server;
  - FPS aimbots: Easy Anti-Cheat at public release;
  - scripts and macros: rate limits only.

## Public release

One server program covers three ways to host:

- a friend hosting from the game, through Steam or Epic relays;
- community servers on Linux;
- official servers as containers on a game hosting service.

At release the game needs:

- Steam or Epic Online Services login;
- UDP through Steam Datagram Relay or EOS relays, which hide IP addresses;
- lobbies and matchmaking;
- Easy Anti-Cheat (free with EOS on Windows, Mac, Linux and Steam Deck);
- replays (seed plus orders) for cheat reports.

Decided now so release stays cheap:

- the connection sits behind one interface;
- a player is an id from a login provider, not a room token;
- every connection starts with a protocol version check;
- the server builds as a plain Linux program that fits in a container, so it can change hosts (Hathora, a game host, shut down in May 2026).

## Rejected (2026-10-11)

- **Lockstep:** every PC would hold the full state (map hacks), the FPS view would lag by the input delay, and Mac and Windows would need bit-identical math.
- **Unreal actors and replication for gameplay:** ties rules to the engine, tests need the editor, and a dedicated Unreal server needs a source-built engine.
- **Bevy client:** weakest where this game is heavy (UI, audio, effects), with breaking releases every four to five months.
- **C++ core:** links into Unreal with no bridge, but data races and memory bugs show up only at runtime. Rust rejects most at compile time, which matters for a multithreaded tick written mostly by agents.
- **Unity:** its Terms of Service (17.2(ff)) bar AI agents and MCP clients except through Unity's own authorized framework.

## Confidence and open risks

| Claim | Confidence | Settled by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rules core outside the engine, server as referee, fog filtering | Very high | It's how the game already works |
| A native server fits more units into each tick | Measured: the straight port of the hot path is about 2 times faster than Node (17.2 ms against 35.7 ms per tick at 2,000 units, Measurements); more needs data layout and the parallel tick | #2 |
| The Rust core links cleanly into Unreal | High | #3 |
| Unreal is the right client (agent speed in Unreal, runtime terrain, crowd cost) | Good, not certain | #3 |
| Thousands of units | Unknown | #2, then the step 2 benchmark |

## Costs

- No playing from a link: Unreal dropped HTML5 export after 4.24.
- Windows builds are made on a Windows PC.
- Unreal 5.8 is the last planned Unreal 5 release; a move to Unreal 6 comes later.
- Two build tools (cargo and Unreal's).
- Determinism needs care: Rust's default hash maps iterate in random order, and neither Rust's platform math nor the `libm` crate gives V8's results (Measurements), so the core carries its own math module.

## Order of work

1. Two tests: #2 (sim) and #3 (Unreal). Decide here: go ahead, change the client, or stop.
2. Rules core and `ww2-server`, measured against the pinned JavaScript as `PARITY.md` describes; benchmark at 400, 1,000 and 2,000 units.
3. Unreal game: terrain, units, effects, HUD, sound, then the FPS view, with the browser client still working alongside.
4. Retire the JavaScript client and Node server in ww2-rts.

## Quiet Conquest opening policy (2026-10-13)

`commander_ai.rs` implements the ordinary Conquest opening point-selection component from `shared/ai.js`, using an owned, validated observation. It preserves the scout aim, income and distance score, headed-unit load, capped failure memory, first infantry holder, busy-unit checks, neutral capture moves, uncapped cut-point attack-moves and cover-cell or circular waypoint selection. Scores and waypoint math use core math. Stable unit IDs and objective order define ties. The source oracle calls the unchanged exported thinker with actual decoded observations, explicit component overlays and a recorded fraction tape; it disables economic branches through the observed zero budget rather than replacing source helpers. The fixture retains pending holder cover/garrison outputs separately and currently records one cover order, so the movement comparison does not imply a complete thinker input log.

`match_commander.rs` is an explicit authority-to-observation boundary. The driver refreshes canonical vision only at source ticks 1, 5, 9 and onward, skipping a pass already applied by another Match caller. Ordinary startup has no initial vision pass. Its fallback vision pass uses a fresh query index and preserves the maintained gameplay index. Delivery requires that canonical phase rather than taking an extra look. The producer reads the recipient's ordered remembered terrain, masks authored mines using their public ground/object layer, and projects source public position, HP, suppression and visible-target precision. Private path and relevant busy-plan facts belong only to the owner. The policy cannot borrow authoritative state. Its two-tick delivered frame remains owned and unchanged between deliveries. Refreshing recipient observation state is separate from publishing commands; queue rejection commits neither seat policy memory nor its purpose RNG.

The bounded driver uses the source scripted planner's easy/normal/hard intervals of 120/40/20 ticks and seat stagger of 13 ticks. It replaces the prototype's load-dependent snapshot cadence with a fixed two-tick beat, and replaces shared `Math.random` with `StreamId::Ai(slot)` from the recorded match seed. These follow the deterministic replacements in PARITY. Commands enter the canonical bounded queue at the next tick boundary with explicit owner/sequence keys, then use the same Match command validator as human moves. A caller must reserve an issuer's sequence space exclusively for this driver. The source's default seat brain is the human-like camera commander; this component does not claim that camera, look, reaction or input-queue behavior.

The driver explicitly defers after the quiet opening, on visible enemy contact or enemy objectives, and for injured, heavily suppressed or unsupported own profiles. It does not shop, spend support, retreat, fight, fortify, run staged assaults, project complete economy/logistics/aircraft/job state, preserve AI state in saves, plan World strategy or schedule a complete Match tick. Positive-budget shopping is a pending policy branch, not a player rule change. Full AI rows remain in progress until those branches and a seeded complete-match input trace are verified.

## Base World geography generation (2026-10-12)

`world_generation` generates the bare geography stage in the core, without file, network or engine access. Huge is 512 by 512 cells with 64 regions; Massive is 1024 by 512 with 128. Each region begins in a 64-cell province. The implementation follows `world-conquest.js`, `world-landforms.js`, `world-roads.js` and the territory growth in `world-territories.js` at the pin: substantial relief with two armor passes, one to three main rivers, zero to three fordable tributaries, a connected lake, two bridges and two fords per main river, guarded objective reserves, a proximity road network, wide road verges, woodland and city blocks, distant homes, unique names and weighted cell membership.

`generate` takes the match's recorded `MatchRandom`, consumes exactly one Terrain draw and retains its low 32 bits as the geography seed. Weather, combat and AI draws cannot affect the result. `generate_from_terrain_seed` replays that explicit geography seed. The source's main Mulberry32, independent hydrology Mulberry32 and independent name LCG operate only within generation. This preserves the landscape algorithms without adopting the prototype's global random stream. Invalid player/team requests draw nothing. Inputs are bounded to one through six seats and team IDs zero through five, consistent with native match inputs.

Core sine, cosine, arctangent, hypot and rounding decide every threshold and route cost. Road costs remain float32, while their heap scores and territory distances remain float64. Score-only heaps, stable proximity sorting and insertion-ordered backbone traversal preserve the source's ties. The source's foliage phase intentionally uses decimal `6.283`; substituting TAU would move woodland thresholds. All output is owned typed data in cell coordinates. `into_world_map_input` moves the terrain and regions into the shared `world_map` records, retaining waterways as authoritative metadata. It leaves layers and biomes absent to select rows-only initialization, and supplies no rails. Loader validation remains a separate dependency. The seed and hydrology diagnostics are authoritative data and do not define a public map response.

The independent recorder invokes the original generator with `scenery: false`, then records ten Huge/Massive maps for seeds 0, 1, 42, 20261003 and 4294967295. Fingerprints cover every terrain character, height and region-map cell; direct metadata comparisons cover regions, homes, teams, names, river path hashes, crossings, lake and passes. A second check uses the source stress tool's 80 settings across both sizes, one through six players and mixed teams, generating each twice. Independent cardinal walks require every region to remain reachable with every bridge destroyed and a three-cell-wide clearance corridor. Channel steps stay contiguous at zero height, tributaries join and widen their parents, homes have neutral expansion 50 through 70 cells away, and comparable flat territory reserves leave at least 20 candidate 3-by-3 building footprints after excluding the home HQ. These are geometric construction checks, not full placement or economic pacing tests. No performance claim is made.

This milestone stops before `dressWorld` and `railNetwork`. Native generator version 1 identifies that partial stage, distinct from the prototype's full generator version 3. Biomes, landmark buildings, scenery isolation, rails, World startup, full construction fairness, privacy projection and multiplayer acceptance remain queued work. Related parity rows stay in progress where those pieces are required. The stage does not alter a balance value, the reference pin, C ABI, rules hash or wire format.

Unit positions, owners, hit points, movement and wallets remain caller-owned. `LogisticsState` is still the single reserve authority; territorial service adds optional `supply_rate` and `cut_for` to that record, initially absent. Store locations are the source's explicit 40-tick synchronization cache.

The `World` adapter supplies current unit facts in authoritative insertion order, physical handoff, territorial supply rates, route planning/continuation and immediate typed spawn, retire and movement effects. Operations must be visible to later queries within the same call. Sources, caches, parked empty halftracks, aid hospitals and depot points retain the source lifecycle, stock order and source refill rules. Private stock excludes grants, and automatic fleets cannot re-carry allied donations. Local service runs before territorial service, including their overlapping refill behavior. The source's constant capacities, dispatch/load/unload intervals and route budget stay beside this module and are checked through original-helper traces rather than a second catalog.

Typed context validates dimensions, owners, finite coordinates/population, nonnegative finite time and a safe JavaScript tick range with room for the longest retry before changing state. Support spending resolves a canonical unit ID and rejects negative or nonfinite amounts before any spending. Unit facts, restored convoy records and low-level store stock remain trusted internal inputs, not an untrusted-save parser. Ordinary movement interception marks the convoy held/manual; the caller applies the ordinary unit order. The unused legacy World region-cache store form is excluded explicitly.

The recorder executes original functions with deterministic route, continuation, handoff and territorial-rate hooks. Twelve Conquest, Classic and World traces cover zero-time setup and 540 runtime steps, plus six payer-pool and five support-spending cases. Complete ordered internal state and two recipient projections are compared, including finite donations, population scaling, clustered member order, route failures/retries, fleet growth/retirement, manual/resume/death, team changes during unloading, on-course route reuse and stuck-route repair. This proves the component for those explicit hooks. It does not implement the supply-network flood, actual safe-routing/handoff algorithms, match orchestration, forced withdrawal, World region-rate projection or persistence/wire serialization. The Rust server is not linked to this component, and no Game fields, ABI or public rules hash change.

## Physical unit reserves (2026-10-13)

`logistics.rs` ports all twelve exported reserve helpers from `shared/logistics.js`. `LogisticsState` stores only the optional reserve record in a `BTreeMap` keyed by unit ID. Owners, type names, positions, hit points and movement remain in their existing state; calls borrow the few unit facts they need. Definition metadata comes from the compiled unit catalog. Reserve constants retain the pinned source values and are checked directly against its `LOGISTICS` export.

Initialization preserves the source eligibility checks and never refills an existing reserve record. Ammo is spent in whole projectiles; supply stores hold ammo credits, including paid fractional credit until a complete projectile can be issued. Provisions, ordinary fuel, emergency fuel, warning time and shortage/recovery latches follow the original operation order. Non-finite or negative count/time/stock inputs receive the source's zero-clamping behavior where its helpers apply that rule. Metadata lookup errors occur before callers mutate reserve state. The numeric definition adapter and owner-controlled reserve access are not arbitrary JavaScript coercion or untrusted-save validation; a persistence loader must validate its own records.

The original JavaScript functions provide 60 enablement contexts, 118 weapon definitions, 708 initialization cases and 44 traces containing 618 exact reserve/stock/query steps. Tests include all 47 unit definitions, fractional volleys and credit, the credit epsilon, exhaustion and recovery boundaries, zero/invalid quantities, riding, actual powered travel time, repeat initialization and stable unit-ID ordering. Convoy routing, stores in the world, territory supply, retreat/path actions, persistence and private snapshot delivery are separate work. This module does not enable logistics in a match or change `Game`, the ABI or the rules hash.

## Weather planning and public helpers (2026-10-13)

`weather.rs` ports map mood/default selection, seeded weather plans, the single planned transition, warning rows, effect descriptions, AI caution and the presentation road mask from `shared/weather.js`. Weather multipliers, their ordering and the warning interval come from the compiled catalog. Existing movement speed and sight functions are unchanged. Plan state is separate from `Game` and can be held by a future match aggregate.

The planner takes an explicit `u32` seed and preserves the reference's private three-draw mulberry32 sequence. It does not consume the new global match streams. A future match initializer can draw and record one plan seed; that integration is not implemented here. `WeatherPlan.at` is a simulation tick, including for map defaults, whose reference helper expresses its transition in seconds. Typed weather names reject unknown values; metadata and lobby-choice adapters retain the reference fallback to the map's default. Road masks require a nonempty rectangular ASCII terrain view and describe the client's road appearance, not simulation road flags.

The fixture calls the original JavaScript helpers for 158 metadata cases, 5,682 seeded/explicit plans, 590 warning and transition rows, every weather description and AI caution value, and 231 synthetic road cases. It checks road-mask fingerprints for all 33 existing public authored-map projections, reusing those committed inputs rather than copying them. Local focused tests compare plans, rows, masks and floating-point AI caution bits exactly. Living rain, wet-ground changes, full match initialization, server snapshots and client integration remain outside this slice.

## Live weather phase

`weather_runtime.rs` supplies the late environment phase as borrowed views of the match's existing seed, wind, shower state and smoke fields. It owns no second copy of the match state. `environment_random` is the shared wrapping mulberry32 draw from the pinned `g.seed`: startup, wind, showers and later fire work must use that same seed, including when showers are disabled. The separate weather-plan seed remains independent.

The order follows `shared/sim.js`: apply the planned weather change near the start of the tick with the existing `WeatherPlan::step`; later, age smoke using the old rain intensity, consume two wind draws, drift every smoke cloud (including one whose lifetime just expired), then update showers, rain intensity and wetness. Rain holds the rainy flag and resets the shower timer; Snow clears the rainy flag without consuming a shower-timer draw; Mud pins wetness to one while showers can still change. Zero elapsed time still consumes the wind draws and can toggle an expired shower timer. One long step toggles at most one shower.

The return value only marks the every-ten-tick fire/flood phase and its `dt * 10` interval. The integrator must check for actual fire/flood work, perform it after weather, and remove expired smoke afterward, so smoke created by fire is not aged immediately. Fire spread, burning damage, flooding, terrain mutation and full Match wiring remain outside this helper. Nonfinite inputs, negative elapsed time and nonfinite results return an error before any borrowed state is changed.

The fixture adds exports to the original pinned module without rewriting its function bodies. It compares 59 sequences and 386 late-phase steps bit for bit, including all five fixed weather kinds, missing plans, disabled showers, 32 seeded random plans, Rain-to-Mud and Fog-to-Clear boundaries, rain/soak thresholds, wind clamps, expired smoke and long/zero time steps. A separate 400-draw check verifies the shared RNG states and results. These are deterministic correctness checks, not performance measurements.

## Deterministic match inputs (2026-10-13)

The core now has versioned random-stream state and a bounded order queue for the future match loop. The seed is recorded once. Terrain, weather, combat, off-map support and each AI seat derive a separate stream from that seed and a stable purpose key. Additional draws by one AI cannot consume another purpose's draws. Version 1 uses the wrapping integer operations in [Sebastiano Vigna's SplitMix64 reference](https://prng.di.unimi.it/splitmix64.c). It generates a 53-bit fraction for game probabilities and uses rejection sampling for bounded integers. This is simulation randomness, not a source for authentication tokens. Unknown snapshot versions and duplicate or unordered stream entries are rejected.

The queue consumes exactly one numbered tick at a time, including empty ticks. Callers assign an authoritative tick, issuer and sequence; accepted orders for that tick apply in issuer/sequence order, independent of their network arrival order. Admission policy is the caller's responsibility; a full queue rejects the next offered order. Capacity is caller-selected, and a rejected duplicate, past-tick or over-capacity order does not alter queued state. Snapshot data preserves the next tick and ordered pending commands. This replaces incidental arrival ordering inside the core; network admission and the complete command schema remain separate work. Neither component exposes a new C or WebSocket interface, and neither is a complete game loop.

Focused tests compare SplitMix64 with values from the compiled C reference, isolate purpose streams, resume streams and queues, permute arrival order, and reject invalid state. Integration with the full match simulation remains pending.

## Match deployment helpers (2026-10-13)

`deployment.rs` provides `spawns_for`, `spawn_distances`, `spawn_slots` and `win_vp` without constructing a match. Terrain is an explicit borrowed view of flags from the original authoring rows and optional levels, before building footprints or later match edits. Spawn filtering retains authoring order and includes Assault-only spawns only for Assault. Distance matrices and selected layouts use indices relative to that filtered list; the caller maps them back to the authoring spawn list. The VP goal reads `CFG.vpToWin` from the compiled catalog and scales by average team size.

Walking distances use east, west, south and north in source order. Entering a ford costs six cells, all other passable cells cost one; MOVE blocks entry, and adjacent levels may differ by at most one. Disconnected pairs use four times the straight-line distance through the core's deterministic `hypot`. Seven circular integer queues preserve the reference bucket insertion order while avoiding a separate queue for every possible accumulated distance. The input size bound keeps every reachable path below the reference's `1e9` infinity threshold.

Layout selection preserves the source's recursive order and pairwise score accumulation: enemy distances add to the score, allied distances subtract, and the nearest enemy pair breaks the tie after the 3% score filter. Both comparisons keep the source's `1e-9` tolerance. Four scans find the best score, best nearest-enemy distance, eligible count and chosen layout without retaining all candidate layouts. At most six players and six spawns are accepted, including shared starts when players outnumber spawns; the largest search is `5^6 = 15,625` layouts. A caller supplies either the first-choice selection or one finite random fraction in `[0, 1)`, drawn from its recorded match stream. There is no hidden draw or global random state.

Three focused tests compare all 33 authored maps plus eight constructed terrain cases, 957 layouts and 18 VP goals against the original JavaScript helpers at `e4e579a`. Cases include every six-player team partition, every supported player/spawn count, asymmetric ford distances, missing heights, cliffs, disconnected islands, shared starts and thresholds on either side of the tolerance. Invalid dimensions, buffer shapes, cells, indices, counts, non-finite/negative distances, score overflow and invalid random fractions return errors. Tiny maps are allowed for component fixtures; the authoring-map loader enforces the game's minimum dimensions.

This is component evidence, not a completed match-start pipeline. The caller still normalizes mode settings, applies the Assault defender-spawn override and Horde/Tutorial shared starts, handles World home assignments, and creates starting units, buildings and wallets. The helpers do not change the map loader, `Game`, the ABI or wire messages.

## Rust lobby and session server (2026-10-12)

`rust/crates/server` now provides `ww2-server`, a standalone HTTP/WebSocket process. Its first slice owns rooms, human and AI seats, observers, lobby settings, token reconnect/takeover, latency ping, a public room directory and cleanup. It does not start or simulate matches. Unsupported match commands return explicit denials, so clients cannot mistake a lobby for a running game.

Axum and Tokio handle transport; pure lobby transitions take an explicit monotonic time and return recipient-specific messages. Each connection has a generation identity. A replaced socket can neither mutate the room nor disconnect its replacement. Tokens stay private and retain their UTF-16 code units during truncation, so two distinct tokens cannot collide through lossy Unicode conversion. Name display at a split surrogate remains a documented difference in the server README.

Host authority follows the reference, including a spectator hosting an all-AI lobby. Directory entries require a listed room and a connected human seat. Disconnected seats remain for ten seconds; empty rooms expire after sixty. Each client has a 64-message output queue, with a slow client closed using 1013. Incoming messages are capped at 16 KiB; the current transport sends uncompressed JSON.

The server accepts missing or zero `hello.proto` and refuses unsupported versions. It sends `lobby.proto: 0`; no rules hash is advertised before a rules core is linked. The pending in-match privacy proposals are unchanged. Binding keeps the reference `HOST`/`PORT` default of `127.0.0.1:3000`, with `WW2_BIND` and then `--bind` as explicit overrides.

The live harness compares 38 lobby/directory checkpoints against the real Node server and checks all 33 map-catalog entries. It also checks version refusal, malformed input recovery, explicit start denial and oversized-message closure. Nine Rust tests cover settings, authority, identity, cleanup, limits and configuration. This is lobby compatibility for the tested cases, not full protocol or multiplayer-match completion.

The server also embeds the client-safe projection of all 33 authored maps. The generator calls the pinned reference's `mapForClient` and refuses a changed source tree. The binary serves those JSON bytes without Node or a reference checkout; it contains no raw authoring map route. Mines and their hidden material rows, triggers and scenario scripts are excluded. These projections cannot initialize an authoritative match. All editor-header map reads return 403, and map writes return 405 until the editor and full-world loader are built. A second live harness matches 96 HTTP responses against Node, including both URL forms, invalid paths, methods and credential refusal; two focused Rust tests check the embedded data and routing. Static browser hosting, map editing, authoritative world loading, compression, operatives, game simulation, snapshots and persistence remain missing.

## Combat damage and suppression component (2026-10-13)

`rust/crates/core/src/combat.rs` evaluates projectile arrival damage and suppression from explicit combat inputs. It also provides role, armor-facing, veterancy, retreat-protection, bunker-scaling and recent-threat helpers. Unit definitions and constants come from the compiled catalog; technology modifiers reuse `economy::tech_mul`, and bearings use the core's deterministic math. No fields are added to `Game`.

The component returns ordered `CombatEvent` values instead of mutating an incomplete match state. Damage events retain health changes, rider reactions, last hitter, death impulse, retarget reset, hit source and time, anti-tank hit time, and shooter XP. Suppression events retain the shared suppression-set insertion, the capped suppression value and hit memory. Building damage deliberately replaces the earlier AP, retreat and veterancy calculation before technology, matching the source. Zero damage still has the source's rider and hit-memory effects; already-dead targets emit none.

Rider events are requests for the later transport integrator. In original cargo order, an existing rider is removed from all copies in the carrier's cargo, has `riding` cleared, moves to the centre of its nearest free cell using its own movement block mask, updates the spatial index, and receives at least 60 suppression. This normal disembark does not clear its orders, path or targets, cause injury, drown it, or emit a shot. A missing rider ID remains in cargo in the source; the request contract preserves that detail. Terrain placement and grid mutation are not implemented by this component. Suppression takes the already evaluated `coverMul` and `coverBehind` values and combines them in source order; terrain cover sampling remains separate.

`harness/combat-fixture.mjs` exposes private functions through an export-only loader and executes their unchanged bodies at reference `e4e579a` under x64 Node 24.21.0. Property proxies record the actual mutation order. Six focused tests pass in debug and release on the Mac against 2,861 helper calls, 741 damage cases and 226 suppression cases. Coverage includes AP and naval restrictions, buildings and structures, technology, retreat, veterancy thresholds, zero damage, already-dead targets, overkill XP, rider requests, retaliation and duplicate suppression. The generator verifies the pin and clean tracked reference and reproduces its fixture with `--check`. Strict core Clippy and formatting pass. This component does not fire weapons, select targets, choose collisions, sample terrain cover, apply its events, remove dead units or implement blasts; the affected combat parity rows remain in progress.

## Capture points and point supply phases (2026-10-13)

`objectives.rs` owns the canonical objective record and two standalone phases: sequential capture-point updates and point-supply connectivity. Ordered unit facts carry the live unit's owner, kind, position, HP, riding, retreating and forced-reserve state; player facts carry team, eliminated state and spawn. The capture pass records qualifying unit IDs and contest status before handling the first qualifying player's team, prerequisite ownership, neutralization and capture progress. It uses the compiled catalog's infantry definitions, capture time and radius. A prerequisite captured earlier in the same point list is immediately usable; a later prerequisite waits until the next pass.

Capture completion returns an ordered event instead of updating the story or notifying clients. The match integrator must stamp capture time and tally the event only while undecided, as `story::captured` does. Capture state itself is not gated by a winner in the source. Ownership, progress and point order preserve the source calculations; no winner or income rule is implemented here.

Point supply recomputes enemy control and reached cells from an explicit terrain view, player spawns and the current unit facts. It uses `SpawnPlacer::nearest_free` with the source's MOVE-only seed mask, then floods left, right, up and down through cells free of MOVE and VBLOCK with height steps at most one. The seed itself remains reached even if closed or vehicle-blocked. Armed enemy ground units close an 8 m circle, except within 16 m of held points; retreating, riding, airborne and dead units do not close it, while forced-reserve or eliminated-player units still can. A point is supplied when any reached cell lies in its 8 m capture square. These circular-control and square-connectivity checks intentionally remain distinct. Neutral points have their cut flag cleared. Team processing retains first-held-point order. No hidden cache or terrain mutation is used.

The checked API validates the complete input set before changing objective records; supply flags are committed after all teams finish. `harness/objective-fixture.mjs` executes the unchanged capture statements extracted from `step` and the original `zocClosed`/`supplyLines` functions at reference `e4e579a`, with x64 Node 24.21.0. Four focused tests compare 214 capture traces (1,165 checkpoints) and 223 supply states, including exact progress bits, capture events, closed/reached masks and cut flags. Cases cover contesting, allies, ordered prerequisites, every unit type, forced reserves, bridges, elevation, free-zone boundaries, blocked seeds and naval blockers. Debug and release tests, strict core Clippy and formatting pass on the Mac. Phase scheduling, disabled-mode handling, income, territory refill networks, match integration and winner/loss rules remain separate work.

## Wallet, population and income state (2026-10-12)

`economy_state.rs` owns each player's wallet, income readouts and VP. It borrows an ordered view of units, building queues, pending drops, capture points, depots and World regions. The player vector index is the slot. This keeps the operations independent of the legacy `Game` and lets a future match runner supply authoritative state directly. World node-to-region resolution belongs to that runner; this module requires explicit regions and does not infer territory from hidden global state. The catalog now contains 47 tables, including the original exported `WORLD_TUNING`.

Population includes owned field units even when their hp is zero but they remain in the unit collection, queues only on structures, and incoming support units until their drop becomes live. Caps use the selected army size. World caps subtract all team seats from owned regions, split growth among seats not marked out, clamp before army scaling, then round. An away seat still participates in that split. A recipient-only World cap is returned unchanged.

The income phase preserves the reference's order: the leading VP total is captured before the player loop, each default-mode player's VP changes during the loop, and catch-up reads the updated team total. `Mode::Default` represents the absent mode object used by normal Conquest. Explicit Conquest, Tutorial and unknown mode objects retain the Assault fallback. Classic and World use living-unit upkeep and finished, living, owned depots; World additionally requires the depot's region to belong to its owner's team and splits regional income among teammates not marked out, including away teammates. Away or out players receive no income. Starting balances, wave and kill rewards, capture, elimination and production are outside this phase.

Three focused tests compare 37 original-JavaScript traces comprising 217 income steps and 865 player states, including all four army sizes, the seven game modes, absent and unknown modes, cutoff points, mixed teams, queues, drops, depot changes and World territory changes. Three additional World cap cases cover the clamp, eliminated teammates and fewer owned regions than seats; recipient previews and invalid-context errors are checked too. An independent review found that grouping a city's base and bonus changed the last bit: with two ordinary regions followed by a city, the source returns `5.550000000000001` MP/s. The regression now records that original-source result, and the implementation adds each base and bonus separately in source order.

Invalid slots or region indices, duplicate unit IDs, unknown catalog names, non-finite input and negative dt return errors before a wallet changes. This is a deliberate typed-input boundary in place of unchecked JavaScript objects. The fixture calls the unchanged source income block and `worldIncome` at `e4e579a`; it is component evidence, not a running match or end-to-end mode proof. Full economy and mode rows stay in progress. The server, wire snapshots, ABI and formation-only rules hash are unchanged.

## Production and research ownership (2026-10-13)

`production.rs` owns one paid-job vector and head progress value per building ID, plus each player's `TechState` and ordered research jobs. Queue types and active/waiting status are derived from that one vector. Unit ownership, HP, construction progress and ordering are borrowed for every operation; positions and authoritative unit state are never copied into the production state. Wallets stay in `EconomyState`. A new state takes the initial technology values and starts with no building entries; `initialize_building` creates an empty queue with zero progress explicitly, and first use can initialize an entry lazily. Reinitialization preserves existing paid work.

Construction-mode recruitment in Classic and World preserves faction, naval, tier, currency, population and unit-limit checks before selecting a producer. It uses the canonical queues when calculating population. An explicit producer is honored, otherwise the shortest eligible own queue wins with source-order ties; ordinary queues stop at five jobs. The reference's queue selector does not check producer HP, although cancellation and training require a living producer. The component preserves that edge behavior. Access and lab queries separately preserve Horde shared facilities, while ownership of queued units and refunds stays with the paying player.

Training emits at most one completed-unit request per building per advance, resets progress to zero and discards excess time. The match runner must create and place that unit, apply rally orders and initialize other unit systems. Research advances first, pauses while its HQ or Armories are missing, and resumes with progress retained. Armories run non-tier jobs in queue order up to available capacity. Away players continue research; out players stop it. Existing research continues during Classic Sudden Death even though new requests are refused. The match runner calls `clear_queues` once at the Sudden Death transition to clear production with no refund, matching the source.

Paid job IDs are monotonic and stay within JavaScript's safe-integer range. Cancelling a waiting job refunds its stored original charge, keeps the head's progress and returns the refund for the caller's statistics update. The low-level `record_paid` hook records an already-paid job, for example World recovery, without debiting a wallet or doing purchase admission. A queue-only import preserves matching positional identities and charges, assigning zero-charge IDs to changed entries as `productionJobs` does. Import/recovery queues have an explicit 4,096-job resource bound; normal purchase queues retain the source's five-job limit. Invalid inputs leave canonical queues and wallets unchanged.

Two focused tests compare 12 original-source traces with 114 actions and 922 advance calls, including repeated 0.05-second progress, stored-charge refunds, queue reconciliation, cap/limit denials, missing and parallel labs, Horde access, World currency and Sudden Death. The oracle executes the unchanged production/research functions and command branches, with unit creation replaced only by typed completion recording. Completion placement, instant recruitment, building creation/destruction, statistics, persistence and public snapshots/ABI remain outside this slice. The server continues to refuse match start until the complete runtime is ready.

## Conquest recruitment transactions (2026-10-13)

`ProductionState::prepare_recruit` admits instant recruitment for absent-mode Conquest (`Mode::Default`) and explicit `Mode::Conquest`. It borrows ordered authoritative unit facts, canonical queues and the existing `EconomyState`, preserving faction/classic/naval/tier checks, then MP, Fuel, population and unit-limit denial order before maker selection. Prices, caps, population weights and limits come from the compiled catalog and existing economy functions. The first eligible living, finished own maker wins in source order unless `from` names a specific eligible maker. Invalid `from` returns `needs`; teammates' buildings do not serve Conquest purchases. Instant recruitment does not create production jobs.

Preparation returns a non-cloneable `PreparedRecruit` with an immutable request containing building ID, owner, kind and spend. It holds the wallet exclusively and borrows production and context until commit or drop, preventing wallet or canonical queue changes through those references. The caller stages placement, ID allocation and routing before consuming `commit`, then publishes the staged unit without further fallible work. Commit debits MP exactly once and returns `CompletedRecruit`; dropping the token after failed placement leaves the wallet untouched. This moves source payment into the caller's successful placement transaction without adding another wallet or copying authoritative positions/health. The caller must keep the authoritative facts behind its view stable and process recruitment serially. Statistics use the returned spend.

One focused test compares 266 commands executed by the unchanged original buy branch at `e4e579a`, covering all 47 unit types across four factions, tier and denial precedence, exact MP balances, maker order and explicit selection, dead/unfinished and allied makers, queues, pending drops, fractional population and army sizes. ## Authoritative ordinary-map loading (2026-10-12)

`map::AuthoritativeMap::from_json` accepts original authoritative JSON bytes supplied by its caller. The core performs no file, network or engine I/O. It validates ordinary legacy maps and version-2 layers, retains the complete original JSON, and exposes typed spawns, capture points, buildings, legacy triggers and normalized layers. This is separate from the server's public map projections. Those projections have already lost hidden mines, materials and scripts; the format has no provenance marker, so the caller must guarantee that the input is the original authoritative document.

`initialize_terrain` uses `Rules::compiled` and the compiled catalog to build physical flags, optional height levels, house kinds, cell HP, stone-bridge toughness, deterministic starting wear, trench directions and naval shoals. Mines remain a separate layer, so their presence does not replace the underlying physical flags. Material maps use ordered keys. `TerrainState::query_game` supplies the existing movement, vision and navigation query state, with players, units and structural sections empty. It does not create a playable match or initialize structural graphs, scenario execution, mode state or match randomness.

The first ordinary-map stage returned `Unsupported` for every `world` or `scenario` property. Generated World support is now described below; authored scenarios still return `Unsupported`, including empty values. Authored structures are validated by the structural slice below. Legacy timed triggers are retained and checked against their migrated scenario bounds, but no trigger executes. Invalid supported fields return field-specific errors, without promising the JavaScript's exact error strings. JSON input is capped at 16 MiB before parsing; this is a core resource bound, separate from the reference editor's 8 MB HTTP limit. No server endpoint or C interface changes in this slice.

It executes the original `createGame` initialization statements up to height initialization, then returns before structural setup, starting units and mode changes. The fixture includes the 1024 by 1024 size limit and Unicode string-length cases.

Issue #35 tracks this slice. The local workspace tests, strict Clippy, formatting and fixture regeneration checks pass on macOS. ## Layered generated World loading (2026-10-13)

`AuthoritativeMap` now accepts original generated World maps through the existing in-memory JSON validator. `world_map::WorldMapInput` provides the native generator a typed handoff for cell characters, optional heights, explicit normalized layers, spawns, landmark building tags and geography. Absent typed layers explicitly selects the source's rows-only migration. The handoff represents generated terrain, geography and landmark tags, not arbitrary authoring documents with authored structures or triggers; those remain supported through original JSON. No client projection is consulted or repaired into authoritative input.

Immutable `WorldDefinition` retains region vector order, cell-space sites and bounds, one home index per spawn, optional names/kinds/biome labels/team hints, the membership vector, biome bytes, seed/version and uninterpreted extra metadata. Membership indexes the source region vector; IDs are unique but are neither sorted nor reassigned. Rail and waterway metadata are retained for later systems without validating or executing their algorithms. `World::from_map` keeps this geography apart from canonical mutable `Game` terrain. Team hints remain authoring metadata, not live ownership. Regions, player homes, capture progress, defenders, rail state and other World mode startup are not initialized. Ordinary `StartPlan::prepare` explicitly refuses World maps rather than constructing Conquest from them.

World validation preserves the source's 1-6 spawn and zero-point rules, 64/128 region counts, 64-cell span, optional per-cell membership with indexes -1 through count-1, unique IDs/homes, open objective sites and one home per spawn. The connectivity walk starts at the first objective, visits east, west, south, north, refuses MOVE or VBLOCK cells and height steps greater than one, and must reach every objective. This is the map validator's connectivity rule. The generator's stronger corridor and bridge-destruction checks remain separate. Huge/Massive dimensions are not inferred or forced by the validator, matching the source's acceptance of authored dimensions within 20-1024 cells.

Malformed World inputs now return field-specific errors instead of the previous unsupported boundary. Defensive checks additionally constrain region IDs/team hints to i32, seed/version to u32, bounds to ordered in-map integers, biomes to one byte per cell, and optional kind/name/biome to text. The source validator does not fully check those fields. Any present `world` field, including null or false, selects native World validation and is rejected if malformed; the source can treat those falsy values as ordinary maps. Typed metadata cannot replace reserved geography fields, and supplied normalized material maps must match the composed layers. Construction returns a fresh value only after validation; no existing World is partially changed. JSON input retains its 16 MiB bound. File reads are bounded separately in `simtest::map::load`, exposed by `simtest --map`; the core does no file I/O.

The existing authoritative-map oracle now records 138 cases with 58 exact static terrain states: all 33 authored maps, the earlier boundaries, four bare/dressed Huge/Massive generated worlds, five synthetic World boundaries and 23 new source validation failures. The former empty-World unsupported case is now a validation failure. All other 105 earlier case records remain unchanged. Lossless run encoding reduces fixture size while retaining complete input membership/biomes and exact terrain arrays, materials and float bits. Typed tests cover canonical layer transfer, malformed inputs and the ordinary-startup refusal. This is component validation/loading evidence, not a generated Match, running server, wire change or Unreal integration. Eight focused map/world/structural tests, two ordinary startup tests, strict workspace Clippy and formatting pass.
